column1: i,ɪ|Compare repeated models|Listen three times: first for meaning, then the vowel, then the final consonant. Make your own take after the third hearing.|What changes across your listens?|The feature you attend to|The target recording
ɛ,æ|Remember one hearing|Hear the model once, pause, and reproduce it before replaying. Compare the feature you remembered.|What should you do before replay?|Try the remembered sound|Read the key
u,ʊ|Hear a word internally|Look at its IPA in silence, imagine the sound, then play the model and compare.|Which step tests internal imaging?|Predict before playback|Repeat during playback

p,b|Interpret a silent model|Use the chart's lip diagram without audio. Mime the closure, choose a plausible sound, then listen.|What cannot be determined from closed lips alone?|Whether the stop is p or b|That the lips meet

i,u|Alternate imagined and audible models|Imagine food, say it softly, and listen to the reference. Repeat with seat.|What provides your comparison?|Your prediction and the model|Microphone volume alone
f,v|Mime contact before voicing|Watch yourself mime the lip contact. Add breath and then voice while keeping contact steady.|Which sound adds voice?|v|f
aʊ|Use gesture to recall movement|Sweep your hand as the vowel moves in now. Repeat with no gesture and compare.|Which gesture fits a glide?|One continuous sweep|Two separate taps
θ|Find a nonverbal cue|Choose a mirror, touch cue or simple sketch to remember the dental position. Test it after a pause.|What does the cue recall?|A movement to try|A numeric grade
æ|Introduce a vowel by mime|Form the vowel in bad in a mirror, look away, then produce it. Alternate with bed.|Which comparison reveals a jaw change?|bad and bed|bad and bat
oʊ,aʊ|Model a diphthong silently|Mime the two endpoints in slow motion, blend them and speak. Record both attempts.|What should the blended version contain?|One moving vowel|Two syllables

aɪ,eɪ|Build a glide from two positions|Hold the start, move to the end, then shorten the transition into one syllable.|Which is the production goal?|Smooth continuous movement|Two isolated vowels with silence
eɪ,i|Say letter names and their sounds|Give the names A and B, then identify the vowel sounds in those names. Compare name and word usage.|Which vowel occurs in the name B?|i|ɛ
p,t,k|Introduce a consonant through its closure|Mime three closures and attach the same vowel to each. Listen to the resulting words.|Which closure uses both lips?|p|t
s,z|Find a voiced partner on the chart|Select s, then its voiced partner. Sustain each before placing it in a word.|Which symbol pairs with s for voicing?|z|ʒ

f,v|Associate a gesture with voicing|Use a fingertip at the throat as a reminder to switch voice on. Alternate fan and van.|What remains similar in the change?|The lip–teeth narrowing|The presence of voicing

p,b,i|Compare cues around a stop|Record cap and cab. Attend to the preceding vowel as well as the final consonant.|Which can help distinguish the endings?|Preceding vowel duration|How many letters you type
ʃ,tʃ|Mime closure versus friction|Model ship and chip silently, then record them. Make closure and release visible in your gesture.|Which starts with closure?|chip|ship
m,n,ŋ|Sort consonants by movement|Organize three nasal sounds by place of closure and test your order by saying them.|What is the front-to-back order?|m n ng|ng n m

l,ɹ|Make one self-correction|Choose one uncertain target, predict one change, record and compare. Keep a note of the useful cue.|Which instruction is more actionable?|Touch the ridge for the l in lane|Speak perfectly
i,ɪ|Read a silent sound sequence|Tap the sounds of seat on the chart, wait, then blend them aloud without reading the spelling.|Which symbol comes between s and t in seat?|i|ɪ

eɪ|Infer possible spellings from a sound|Hear the word and suggest a spelling. Think of a different spelling for the same vowel.|Which two words share a vowel despite different spellings?|day and eight|day and did

ə,stress|Save a word with its pronunciation|Add an expression to My Words with a context that clarifies its reading. Retrieve it from IPA later.|Which helps disambiguate record?|A sentence using the word|Only its letter count
i,ɪ|Transcribe from ordinary spelling|Read the printed word, build its IPA, then listen and correct a single symbol.|Which is a transcription of sit?|/sɪt/|/sit/

ɛ,æ|Use a spelling error as a listening clue|Compare a mistaken guess with the reference word. Identify whether the confusion is sound or spelling.|Does one misspelling prove a pronunciation error?|No|Yes
ʃ|Collect words sharing one sound|Say ship, cash and machine. Identify the same consonant in different positions and spellings.|What is shared by all three?|ʃ|tʃ
i,ɪ,ɛ|Build a three-way contrast|Say seat, sit and set in separate requests. Check which single sound changes.|Which position changes?|The vowel|The first consonant

longstress|Describe a stress decision|Predict the strong syllable, then record and compare with a model. Describe what you heard.|Which is an observation rather than a spelling clue?|A longer or more prominent syllable|A capital letter in a heading
stress|Try different cues for stress|Record a word three times, changing length, pitch and loudness separately. Compare their effects.|Can pitch and duration both contribute?|Yes|No
syllables|Represent syllables with objects|Lay out a coin or finger for each syllable of banana. Make the middle marker stand out.|How many markers do you need?|Three|Two
longstress|Move the main beat experimentally|Say develop with the beat on each syllable, then return to the reference reading.|Where does the reference place the beat?|Second syllable|Last syllable

family|Read your own stress profile|Tap a strong and light pattern for a word. Replay and compare the taps to the recorded word.|What should the markers represent?|Syllables and their relative prominence|One marker per letter
family|Mark two strengths in a long word|Transcribe photographic using primary and secondary marks and compare both beats.|Which mark precedes the primary stressed syllable?|ˈ|ˌ

longstress|Group words with the same beat|Compare develop and remember by tapping their three syllables. Record a third word with that pattern.|What do develop and remember share?|A main beat on syllable two|The same final consonant

stress,family,syllables|Sort several stress profiles|Group noun record, technique and photography by syllable count and beat. Check one word in a fresh sentence.|Which word has four syllables in the reference?|photography|technique
i,clusters|Count sounds on fingers|Assign a finger to each sound in seat. Touch each one as you blend the word.|How many sound positions are in seat?|Three|Four
clusters|Correct just the missing sound|Build help on your fingers, then say it in a request. If the final closure disappears, return to its finger.|Which position contains p?|The last|The first
link|Track words with fingers in speech|Touch one finger for each word in pick it up while making a connected spoken group.|What should the fingers count here?|Words|Syllables inside pick

group|Shape a phrase with your hand|Move your hand through a phrase, stop at a thought boundary and resume. Record two groupings.|Where does a helpful boundary go?|Between meaningful groups|After every spelling unit
stress|Use a dictionary reading in context|Compare the two readings of record. Save a sentence that makes its part of speech clear.|Which goes with a noun in this example?|Initial stress|Final stress

ɝ,ə|Read a dictionary-style entry|Find the stress mark and vowel before saying the model. Compare British and American notation where supplied.|What does a stress mark normally precede?|The stressed syllable|The whole definition
p,b,m|Read what the lips can show|Mime pin, bin and men without voice. Guess from appearance, then listen and revise.|Can one closed-lip picture identify all three sounds?|No|Yes

t,k|Hide the visible part of a word|Try to distinguish two words with little visible lip motion. Add sound and check the extra information.|Which gives access to voicing and acoustic detail?|Listening|Lip appearance alone

reduction|Hear a careful and a conversational form|Make two versions of next week. Keep the intended date recoverable after the reduction.|What matters in the faster version?|The listener can recover the plan|Every consonant has a strong release
link|Mark joins on replay|Listen to pick it up, mark where sounds cross written boundaries, then repeat without breaking the group.|Which joins naturally?|pick it|a forced pause after pick

reduction|Try three degrees of simplification|Record a careful, comfortable and deliberately over-reduced line. Decide which remains easy to understand.|Which version is the practice target?|Comfortable and intelligible|The fastest possible

rhythm|Contrast flat and selective stress|Read a two-sentence message with equal beats, then emphasize the news. Compare what stands out.|What can selective stress reveal?|The important information|The exact spelling
rhythm|Chant with steady main beats|Tap two beats and fit extra light syllables between them. Return to conversational speech.|Which material can fit between taps?|Light words|Only silent gaps
weak|Add light words without losing the beat|Start with drive home. Add I can before it while keeping drive and home clear.|Which word can weaken in the longer line?|can|home when it carries focus

emphasis|Compare loudness and focus|Record the same answer with more volume throughout, then with one prominent word. Compare the meaning.|Which more directly singles out a detail?|Selective prominence|Turning up the whole recording

rhythm|Build a rhythmic line from symbols|Tap a short original line on the chart, mark two main beats and speak it from memory.|What should you recall between beats?|The lighter syllables|Only isolated loud words
rhythm|Echo the rhythm of a model|Listen without the text, tap the beats, then echo and check where your timing changes.|What should you listen for first?|The pattern of beats|Every letter name
rhythm|Speak alongside a model|Listen, then shadow the modeled line while tapping. Make a solo take and compare.|Which recording lets you hear yourself clearly?|The solo take|Only the model

group|Mime a rhythm before speaking|Trace one gesture for each thought group, then supply the words at the same points.|What can gesture help you remember?|Grouping and prominence|A compulsory pitch range

given|Represent a sentence with markers|Assign markers to the words and enlarge the one introducing the news. Change the question and move it.|Which word should the larger marker follow?|The intended focus|Always the last function word
rhythm|Find the rhythm in a new sentence|Mark a line before hearing the model. Replay, compare, then try an alternative context.|Can two different patterns fit different contexts?|Yes|No

story|Use recording as a private practice lab|Record a story, isolate one short group by replay, improve one feature and return to the full story.|What is the manageable correction unit?|One short group|Every feature at once

group|Try three thought-group readings|Say one message as a single group, as a time plus action, and with an awkward split. Compare meaning.|Which preserves the time expression?|After work / call me|After / work call me

group|Distinguish useful and awkward boundaries|Read a route and insert a pause inside one place name. Move it outside the name on the second take.|Which is easier to recover?|The uninterrupted place name|A split inside the name

story|Invent a grouping for your own story|Tell the same two events with different boundaries and listen for which order is clearest.|What should a helpful grouping preserve?|The order of ideas|Equal word counts

story|Mark groups in a recorded passage|Hear the model without reading, mark where an idea ends, then record a new passage with similar groups.|Which is evidence of an idea boundary?|Meaning supported by timing and pitch|Any brief silence by itself

group|Review rhythm in your own reply|Record a spontaneous arrangement, replay it and choose one boundary to improve.|Which comparison uses your own evidence?|Two recordings of your reply|Two unrelated spellings

weak|Contrast strong and weak readings|Record an offer with light can and a correction with strong can. Compare against both models.|Which is likely to keep the fuller vowel?|Correcting CAN|A neutral unstressed can

continue|Pause before giving the answer|Listen, leave a short thinking pause, rehearse internally and answer once. Compare a rushed version.|What does the pause give you?|Planning time|A guaranteed correct accent

attitude|Notice intonation in your first language|Say a surprised check in Vietnamese, then a calm acknowledgment. Trace both contours and describe the intention.|What are you comparing?|How you used pitch for two intentions|How to convert every tone literally into English

checking|Notice your English intonation|Repeat the two intentions in English using really. Replay both and label them.|What distinguishes the task from reading a question mark?|You have an intended situation|Only the punctuation matters

asking|Listen to another speaker's intention|Hear both models without watching the line. Predict which checks information before revealing context.|Which gives the first clue?|The recorded delivery|The file name

attitude|Listen again after imagining a response|Record a remark, imagine the listener's response, then give it a second reading. Compare the attitude.|What is your second take exploring?|How delivery changes interpretation|A different spelling
i,u,checking|Separate vowel quality from pitch|Sustain one vowel on two notes and then two vowels on one note. Compare the dimensions.|Can the same vowel be produced on different notes?|Yes|No
checking|Extend awareness with replay|Record one question, trace the ending, then record a narrower range. Check by listening.|What changed between versions?|Pitch range|Number of words

quote|Rehearse two sides of a dialogue|Play both roles in a short booking exchange, changing focus when a detail is corrected.|How can one learner do this alone?|Alternate roles and replay|Wait for a teacher to speak both parts

group|Read aloud in sense groups|Mark boundaries in your own two-line announcement, say it, then move one boundary and compare.|Which grouping helps a listener?|Related words kept together|A break every two words

story|Group a spontaneous answer|Answer a question about your weekend without a script. Replay and locate one complete thought.|Which counts as a thought group?|One coherent idea|A fixed number of syllables

story|Retell a personal anecdote|Record a beginning, change and outcome. Retell to an imagined friend using fewer, clearer groups.|What should remain recoverable?|What happened and in what order|The original wording exactly

instructions|Reconstruct a message by listening|Hear the route, write the key details from memory, replay only the missed detail, then give it in your own words.|What determines success here?|Recovering the intended route|Matching every filler word
